bibl.title: UniProt: the universal protein knowledgebase in 2021

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: A KNOWLEDGEBASE THAT DELETES FROM ITSELF AND KEEPS WHAT IT DELETED - 190 million protein sequences in two provenance tiers, with a separate archive holding everything the knowledgebase has dropped
span.quote: The UniProt Knowledgebase (UniProtKB) combines reviewed UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot entries, to which data have been added by our expert biocuration team, with the unreviewed UniProtKB/TrEMBL entries that are annotated by automated systems. The UniRef databases cluster sequence sets at various levels of sequence identity and the UniProt Archive (UniParc) delivers a complete set of known sequences, including historical obsolete sequences.

span.label: what UniProt now contains, how completeness and quality are assessed, and how annotations are evidenced
span.quote: The aim of the UniProt Knowledgebase is to provide users with a comprehensive, high-quality and freely accessible set of protein sequences annotated with functional information.

span.label: a two-year status report: proteome completeness metrics, automated annotation, a credit-based community submission route, and a COVID-19 curation portal
span.quote: To enable researchers to evaluate proteome completeness and expected gene content, we have adopted the BUSCO (Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs) scoring method for vertebrate, arthropod, fungal, and prokaryotic organisms on the Proteomes portal, in addition to providing details of species and the protein count. BUSCO v3 ( 9 ) identifies complete, duplicated, fragmented, and potentially missing genes by comparison to a defined set of near-universal single copy orthologs. As a result of our adoption of the BUSCO algorithm, a number of incomplete and poor-quality proteomes were identified and removed from UniProtKB.

span.label: method
span.quote: The UniProt Knowledgebase (UniProtKB) combines reviewed UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot entries, to which data have been added by our expert biocuration team, with the unreviewed UniProtKB/TrEMBL entries that are annotated by automated systems. The UniRef databases cluster sequence sets at various levels of sequence identity and the UniProt Archive (UniParc) delivers a complete set of known sequences, including historical obsolete sequences.

span.label: protein knowledge as something that must be tiered by provenance, judged for completeness against neighbours, and deleted without being lost
span.quote: As previously described ( 3 ), we continue to remove almost identical proteomes of the same species from UniProtKB ( https://www.uniprot.org/help/proteome_redundancy ), leaving only a relevant representative proteome in that section of the database. The redundant proteome sequences are available through UniParc to researchers and stable proteome identifiers (of the form UPXXXXXXXXX, where Xs are integers) are maintained for each redundant proteome to ensure findability.

span.label: description of a curated resource: expert biocuration for reviewed entries, rule-based automation for unreviewed ones, BUSCO and an in-house detector for proteome quality
span.term: description of a curated resource: expert biocuration for reviewed entries, rule-based automation for unreviewed ones, BUSCO and an in-house detector for proteome quality
span.quote: We also display the results of the ‘Complete Proteome Detector’ (CPD), an in-house algorithm, which statistically evaluates the completeness and quality of each proteome by directly comparing it to those of a group of at least three closely taxonomically related species. The CPD classifies each proteome as either ‘standard’, ‘close to standard’ or an ‘outlier’, according to protein count vs. the standard distribution of protein count expected for completeness in comparison to a cluster of closely related organisms

span.label: IT SOLVES THE PROBLEM THE GENE ONTOLOGY REFUSES. `aleksander2023` in this corpus: the knowledgebase must be `THE CURRENT STATE OF KNOWLEDGE AND NOT JUST AN ARCHIVE OF ALL PUBLIC DATA`. UniProt: `the UniProt Archive (UniParc) delivers a complete set of known sequences, INCLUDING HISTORICAL OBSOLETE SEQUENCES`. **GO REFUSES TO BE AN ARCHIVE; UNIPROT RUNS A SEPARATE ONE SO IT NEED NOT BE**
span.quote: The UniProt Knowledgebase (UniProtKB) combines reviewed UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot entries, to which data have been added by our expert biocuration team, with the unreviewed UniProtKB/TrEMBL entries that are annotated by automated systems. The UniRef databases cluster sequence sets at various levels of sequence identity and the UniProt Archive (UniParc) delivers a complete set of known sequences, including historical obsolete sequences.

span.label: and the deletion is reversible by construction: `we continue to REMOVE almost identical proteomes of the same species from UniProtKB ... The redundant proteome sequences ARE AVAILABLE THROUGH UniParc ... and STABLE PROTEOME IDENTIFIERS ... ARE MAINTAINED for each redundant proteome TO ENSURE FINDABILITY`. Removed from the knowledgebase, kept in the archive, IDENTIFIER PRESERVED
span.quote: As previously described ( 3 ), we continue to remove almost identical proteomes of the same species from UniProtKB ( https://www.uniprot.org/help/proteome_redundancy ), leaving only a relevant representative proteome in that section of the database. The redundant proteome sequences are available through UniParc to researchers and stable proteome identifiers (of the form UPXXXXXXXXX, where Xs are integers) are maintained for each redundant proteome to ensure findability.

span.label: AND WHETHER A PROTEIN IS KNOWN TO EXIST IS A COUNTING RULE WITH TWO THRESHOLDS: `Peptide identifications CAN BE TAKEN AS EVIDENCE that a protein has been VALIDATED (PE = 1) ... AT LEAST TWO UNIQUE PEPTIDES OF SEVEN AMINO ACIDS OR MORE or, FOR PROTEINS WHERE THIS CANNOT BE ACHIEVED DUE TO SEQUENCE CONSTRAINTS, ONE UNIQUE PEPTIDE OF TEN AMINO ACIDS OR MORE`. The fallback exists because some proteins fail the first rule for reasons that have nothing to do with whether they exist
span.quote: Peptide identifications can be taken as evidence that a protein has been validated (PE = 1) using a variation of the HPP guidelines (in brief, at least two unique peptides of seven amino acids or more or, for proteins where this cannot be achieved due to sequence constraints, one unique peptide of ten amino acids or more has been mapped to a protein).

span.label: and completeness is judged AGAINST THE NEIGHBOURS: the `Complete Proteome Detector` `statistically evaluates the completeness and quality of each proteome BY DIRECTLY COMPARING IT TO THOSE OF A GROUP OF AT LEAST THREE CLOSELY TAXONOMICALLY RELATED SPECIES`, classifying it as `STANDARD`, `CLOSE TO STANDARD` or an `OUTLIER`
span.quote: We also display the results of the ‘Complete Proteome Detector’ (CPD), an in-house algorithm, which statistically evaluates the completeness and quality of each proteome by directly comparing it to those of a group of at least three closely taxonomically related species. The CPD classifies each proteome as either ‘standard’, ‘close to standard’ or an ‘outlier’, according to protein count vs. the standard distribution of protein count expected for completeness in comparison to a cluster of closely related organisms

span.label: A NEW INSTRUMENT CAUSED DELETIONS FROM THE KNOWLEDGEBASE: `As a result of our adoption of the BUSCO algorithm, A NUMBER OF INCOMPLETE AND POOR-QUALITY PROTEOMES WERE IDENTIFIED AND REMOVED FROM UniProtKB`. The proteomes did not change; the ruler did
span.quote: To enable researchers to evaluate proteome completeness and expected gene content, we have adopted the BUSCO (Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs) scoring method for vertebrate, arthropod, fungal, and prokaryotic organisms on the Proteomes portal, in addition to providing details of species and the protein count. BUSCO v3 ( 9 ) identifies complete, duplicated, fragmented, and potentially missing genes by comparison to a defined set of near-universal single copy orthologs. As a result of our adoption of the BUSCO algorithm, a number of incomplete and poor-quality proteomes were identified and removed from UniProtKB.

span.label: and the object being counted is hedged in its own definition: a proteome is `the complete set of proteins BELIEVED TO BE EXPRESSED by an organism`. Completeness and belief in the same phrase
span.quote: UniProt release 2020_04 contains over 189 million sequence records (Figure 1 ), with >292 000 proteomes, the complete set of proteins believed to be expressed by an organism, originating from completely sequenced viral, bacterial, archaeal and eukaryotic genomes available through the UniProtKB Proteomes portal

span.label: THE TWO TIERS ARE A PROVENANCE DISTINCTION, NOT A QUALITY ONE ON ITS FACE: `UniProtKB COMBINES REVIEWED UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot entries, to which data have been added BY OUR EXPERT BIOCURATION TEAM, with the UNREVIEWED UniProtKB/TrEMBL entries THAT ARE ANNOTATED BY AUTOMATED SYSTEMS`. A user who does not read the tier reads both as the same kind of claim
span.quote: The UniProt Knowledgebase (UniProtKB) combines reviewed UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot entries, to which data have been added by our expert biocuration team, with the unreviewed UniProtKB/TrEMBL entries that are annotated by automated systems. The UniRef databases cluster sequence sets at various levels of sequence identity and the UniProt Archive (UniParc) delivers a complete set of known sequences, including historical obsolete sequences.

span.label: and the scale makes the tiering unavoidable: entries grew `by >65 MILLION RECORDS, AN INCREASE OF >50% IN JUST 2 YEARS`. No biocuration team can review that
span.quote: Collectively, these have already resulted in the number of entries contained in UniProtKB growing by >65 million records, an increase of >50% in just 2 years.

span.label: BUSCO scoring against a defined set of near-universal single-copy orthologs
span.note: eliminates: incomplete proteomes passing as complete - and it worked in the destructive direction: `a number of INCOMPLETE AND POOR-QUALITY PROTEOMES WERE IDENTIFIED AND REMOVED FROM UniProtKB` · outcome: held
span.quote: To enable researchers to evaluate proteome completeness and expected gene content, we have adopted the BUSCO (Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs) scoring method for vertebrate, arthropod, fungal, and prokaryotic organisms on the Proteomes portal, in addition to providing details of species and the protein count. BUSCO v3 ( 9 ) identifies complete, duplicated, fragmented, and potentially missing genes by comparison to a defined set of near-universal single copy orthologs. As a result of our adoption of the BUSCO algorithm, a number of incomplete and poor-quality proteomes were identified and removed from UniProtKB.

span.label: the Complete Proteome Detector, comparing each proteome to at least three closely related species
span.note: eliminates: the absence of a per-organism expectation - there is no independent count of how many proteins an organism should have, so the neighbours supply one · outcome: partial
span.quote: We also display the results of the ‘Complete Proteome Detector’ (CPD), an in-house algorithm, which statistically evaluates the completeness and quality of each proteome by directly comparing it to those of a group of at least three closely taxonomically related species. span.label: labelling every automatic annotation with its evidence and source
span.note: eliminates: the confusion of an inferred annotation with a curated one - `All automatic annotations are LABELLED WITH THEIR EVIDENCE/SOURCE` · outcome: held
